label: The Morse Index Theorem
notes: Spanning printed pages 242 through 252, this chapter answers a counting question for geodesics. We attach to each geodesic a quadratic index form on variation fields, define its index as the largest negative dimension, and prove this integer equals the number of interior conjugate points counted with multiplicity.

label: Setup: The Variational Stage
notes: Fix a geodesic and consider piecewise smooth vector fields along it that vanish at both endpoints. These are the admissible variations whose second-order behavior the second variation formula measures. The whole theorem lives on this vector space, so we pin down its domain before any analysis begins.

label: The Index Form I(V,W)
notes: The index form is the symmetric bilinear form arising from the second variation of energy. It pairs covariant derivatives against a curvature term, so positive curvature pushes the form negative. Understanding when this form fails to stay positive is the entire problem of the chapter.

label: Jacobi Fields and the Index Form
notes: Jacobi fields are exactly the null directions of the index form among fixed-endpoint fields, satisfying the Jacobi equation. Integrating the index form by parts isolates the Jacobi operator, revealing that degeneracy of the form is governed by these solutions of a linear second-order differential equation.

label: Conjugate Points
notes: Two parameter values are conjugate when a nontrivial Jacobi field vanishes at both. Conjugate points are where neighbouring geodesics refocus and where the geodesic stops being a local energy minimizer. Their multiplicity is the dimension of the space of such vanishing Jacobi fields.

label: The Index of a Geodesic
notes: The index is the dimension of a maximal subspace of admissible fields on which the index form is negative definite. It counts independent directions in which the geodesic can be shortened to second order. A priori this number could be infinite; the theorem shows it is not.

label: Nullity and Degeneracy
notes: The nullity is the dimension of the index form's null space, equal to the number of independent Jacobi fields vanishing at both endpoints. Nullity is positive exactly when the final endpoint is conjugate to the start, marking the degenerate geodesics that sit between index jumps.

label: The Morse Index Theorem
notes: The central theorem states the index of the geodesic equals the number of interior conjugate points to the starting point, each counted with its multiplicity. Because conjugate points are isolated on a compact interval, this sum is finite, so every geodesic has finite index.

label: Broken Jacobi Fields Span Negative Directions
notes: The proof builds an explicit negative subspace from Jacobi fields broken at the conjugate points. Each interior conjugate point contributes fields that make the index form strictly negative, giving a lower bound on the index that matches the conjugate count exactly.

label: Monotonicity of the Index
notes: As the endpoint slides outward along the geodesic, the index is a nondecreasing step function of the parameter. It is constant on intervals free of conjugate points and jumps by the multiplicity each time the moving endpoint crosses a conjugate point to the start.

label: Worked Tally Along a Geodesic
notes: Walking a sample geodesic past three conjugate points of multiplicities one, two, and one, the running index climbs from zero to four. This concrete tally shows how the abstract counting theorem becomes an arithmetic of refocusing events along the curve.

label: Synthesis and Consequences
notes: The theorem ties variational stability, curvature, and Jacobi fields into one finite integer. It implies geodesics past their first conjugate point are not minimizing and underlies Morse theory on path spaces, where indices assemble into homology of the loop space.
